Codelco head offices in Santiago. ( Image by Rodrigo Fernández | Wikimedia Commons. )
By: Northern Miner Staff November 6, 2026
Chilean State miner Codelco disclosed a 42,100-tonne copper production overstatement Thursday, the same day a tailings spill halted processing at its Andina operation.
The miner is assessing a potential inventory adjustment of $120 million to $140 million (C$168 million to C$196 million), Chairman Bernardo Fontaine told an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting. The production findings cover 2024 and 2025 and remain preliminary while audits continue.
“For too long, the discussion at Codelco was excessively focused on how many tonnes were produced,” Fontaine said in a Spanish-language statement. “But it’s not about producing for its own sake.”
The accounting failures and spill investigation confront management with tests of both its reporting and environmental safeguards as it works to reverse declining output and rising debt. Fontaine expects copper production to finish slightly above 1.2 million tonnes this year and average about 1.3 million tonnes annually over the next four years, Bloomberg reported.
Duplicate reports
The company’s written account puts the production overstatement at 24,000 tonnes in 2024 and a net 18,100 tonnes last year. Duplicate records also inflated copper inventories by an estimated 15,200 tonnes, it said.
The irregularities included counting material before it qualified as finished production and recording the same copper at more than one division. They also affected employee incentive payments, which Codelco is calculating and seeking to recover, Fontaine said, according to Chilean newspaper Emol.
KPMG is reviewing production records across all divisions for both years, while EY is conducting a forensic investigation into possible duplicate entries. Codelco dismissed eight executives and professionals on Oct. 29 across Chuquicamata, Ministro Hales, Salvador and its corporate offices.
Financial strain
The investigations come as Fontaine reassesses the returns from Codelco’s spending. The company invested $32 billion over the past eight years without reversing its production decline, he told the meeting, according to Emol.
Transfers to the Chilean government totalled $7 billion over the past four years, 43% below the preceding four-year period despite copper prices rising 30%, Fontaine said. Debt increased 50% to finance those contributions, he added.
Codelco is preparing a recovery plan focused on safer, more profitable production, tighter controls and greater discipline in allocating capital. It also intends to pursue growth through public-private partnerships.
Spill inquiry
At Andina, in the Valparaíso region, Codelco stopped the concentrator and tailings transport after detecting an obstruction in a tailings channel early Thursday.
The company subsequently estimated that between one and five cubic metres of tailings reached the Blanco River. It attributed the blockage to an object falling into the channel following a snow slide during thaw conditions, La Tercera reported.
Codelco said testing of the Blanco and Aconcagua rivers found no significant changes in the parameters examined, including pH, conductivity and temperature. The findings don’t establish the spill’s final environmental impact.
Water utility Esval closed its surface-water intake from the Aconcagua as a precaution and activated underground sources and backup systems. It said drinking-water service in Los Andes continued normally.
Chile’s Superintendency of the Environment has opened an investigation and sent inspectors to assess the spill and cleanup.
The regulator gave Codelco two business days to provide technical records, including the volume spilled, water monitoring and emergency measures. A consolidated report on the cause, environmental effects and steps to prevent a recurrence is due next week.

U.S. European Command is calling on troops, family members, and civilian employees to watch for suspicious behavior on and off military installations and to cover their digital tracks while moving around Europe.
Branded “See Something, Do Something,” the initiative is meant “to foster a proactive mindset” toward security and force protection , the command said this week. The announcement comes amid heightened concern about drone incursions and other hybrid threats to U.S. and allied military forces around Europe.
The initiative emphasizes protecting U.S. personnel and their families “as a shared responsibility vital to sustaining long-term combat readiness alongside global partners.” It encourages members of U.S. military communities to stay alert while in crowded public areas, like transit hubs, and report any “unusual behavior or unattended items” to military police or local authorities.
Troops and their families are also “urged” to practice “rigorous digital discipline” by reviewing their social-media privacy settings, disabling geotagging on fitness apps and mobile devices, and avoiding posting information about their locations and travels online. The announcement also cites a recommendation from security experts to vary daily commuting routes, travel times, and off-base activities “to reduce predictability.”
U.S. personnel and their families “are our most precious asset, and their safety is our highest priority,” Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, commander of U.S. European Command, said in the announcement. “By embracing a proactive security mindset and enhancing collective vigilance, we build a stronger force protection environment that keeps us safe and ready.”
European Command did not identify a specific threat that prompted the campaign, but it comes amid increased concern about “hybrid warfare,” — malign activity below the threshold of war that often lacks a clear perpetrator — involving Russia and targeting U.S. forces and NATO allies.
Russian misinformation and intimidation directed against U.S. military personnel and their families using social media and hacking has been a longstanding concern. But since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, that hybrid activity has become more aggressive and disruptive. A number of undersea pipelines and cables have been affected by what Western officials believe to be sabotage; GPS jamming and spoofing are more frequent, and drone incursions around sensitive sites, like military bases and airports, have increased.
In September, Germany accused Russia of orchestrating a failed attack with explosive-laden drones at the Leipzig/Halle Airport, which is a key logistical hub for Western supplies to Ukraine. Later in September, a tip about suspicious vehicles near the airbase RAF Fairford led to the arrest of several men in relation to a suspected terrorist plot in which British officials say Iran may have been involved. The incident prompted the US to remove the B-1 bombers that were stationed at the base.
In October, after the discovery of a drone with a canister of explosives near another German airbase, the German military raised its Russian sabotage threat assessment to “substantial” — its second-highest level — and warned that the threat was no longer confined to facilities where Ukrainian troops were being trained and to major military installations. More than 30,000 U.S. military personnel are stationed in Germany.

VIENNA — Denmark is the latest country to buy Finland’s “Blocker” naval mines, a day after Lithuania decided to go ahead with its own contract for the weapon.
The forces of Finland, where the mines are made, and Estonia already operate the proximity sea mines. Estonia bought them in 2021.
The Danish acquisition will take place as part of a pentalateral joint procurement agreement that includes Finland and Lithuania, as well as Germany and Norway, who have not yet publicly announced a contract to buy the device.
Lithuania’s ministry of defense similarly said that its procurement of Blocker was taking place under the Naval Mines Cooperation, a procurement agreement that grew out of a program launched in 2024.
Aside from joint buying, the NMC agreement is meant to “strengthen cooperation on logistics, training, exercises and the lifespan of the systems,” the Danish ministry of defense said .
The Finnish military signed a contract with manufacturer Forcit Defence in June on behalf of the five countries participating in the NMC’s procurement scheme. The contract was worth “hundreds of millions of Euros,” the Finnish government said.
Ten countries signed the pact’s original declaration of intent: Belgium, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Poland, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Finland and Estonia, all of which are members of NATO.
Germany may still announce a procurement decision this year, German industry publication Hartpunkt reported , citing “well-informed circles.”
“Selecting Finland as the lead nation of the naval mines cooperation project is a reflection of the Finnish Navy’s long-standing capability in naval mining,” the country’s military wrote in a statement.
Forcit Defence advertises the Blocker mine as having the explosive power equivalent to a ton of TNT. It detects ships using a range of sensors.
Naval mines have been front and center in the news this year, with Iran’s use of the technology to block the Strait of Hormuz and hold a large part of global energy supplies hostage in response to the U.S.-Israeli campaign against it.
The Baltic Sea has also become a key point of tension, particularly since 2022, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With Finland and Sweden’s accession to NATO, the sea is now entirely surrounded by the alliance, except for Russia’s Kaliningrad and Leningrad Oblast coasts. This is a strategic headache for Russia, whose ships must pass through the narrow Danish straits and onward through the Kattegat and Skagerrak to reach the open ocean.
Russia has repeatedly warned that it will not accept being cut off from the Atlantic. “If we do not give them a firm rebuff, the British, French and even the Baltic states will soon become so emboldened that they will try to completely block our country’s access to the seas, at least in the Atlantic basin,” said Nikolai Patrushev, President Vladimir Putin’s aide and chairman of Russia’s Maritime Board, in a February interview with Russian newspaper Argumenty i Fakty and reproduced by the Maritime Board of the Russian Federation. “If this situation cannot be resolved peacefully, the Navy will break through and eliminate the blockade.”

Lucid has released a new teaser video of what looks like the Cosmos, its upcoming sub-$50,000 midsize electric SUV and the car that’s supposed to turn Lucid into a volume automaker.

Same design Lucid filed in Europe

The caption talks about “elevating the experience of movement” and says Lucid can’t wait “to share this feeling with even more people.” It doesn’t name the vehicle, but “even more people” is about as subtle a hint at a cheaper model as you can get.
Two frames from the film show the vehicle at dusk. At the rear, “LUCID” is spelled out in red illuminated letters across the tailgate, flanked by thin red light strips, with a spoiler cutting across the base of the rear glass. Up front, a sculpted LED headlight with a row of vertical segments sweeps across a red body panel.

That rear end matches the Cosmos design Lucid registered with the EU Intellectual Property Office in May, which showed the same spelled-out “LUCID” tailgate and rear-glass spoiler. It also lines up with the thin red light strips on the camouflaged Cosmos prototype spotted on Highway 101 in California last month.
A headlight detail from Lucid’s new teaser video (Image: Lucid)
Lucid Cosmos
Lucid unveiled its plans for Cosmos and Earth at its first Investor Day in March . Both ride on the new midsize platform and start under $50,000, roughly half the price of the Gravity.
On paper, the Cosmos is impressive. Lucid claims about 300 miles of range from a 69 kWh pack, thanks to efficiency of up to 4.5 mi/kWh, which it says is 10% better than its closest competitor. It also claims 200 miles of range in 14 minutes of charging, and its new Atlas drive unit has 30% fewer parts and costs 37% less than the Zeus unit in the Gravity.
The problem is timing. Production was supposed to start in late 2026. In August, CEO Silvio Napoli pushed the Cosmos to 2027 , “most likely the second half.”

Tailings deposition at Cuiabá gold mine. ( Image courtesy of AngloGold Ashanti. )
Posted By: Mining.com Staff November 6, 2026
AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU) plans to spend up to $900 million (C$1.26 billion) expanding three operating mines as it targets another 300,000 to 450,000 oz. of annual gold production by 2030.
The three-year investment budget ranges from $750 million to $900 million and covers Geita in Tanzania, Siguiri in Guinea and Cuiabá in Brazil, the company said in its quarterly results Thursday. Obuasi’s ongoing ramp-up in Ghana forms a separate part of the growth strategy.
“These are high-return, capital efficient projects at our operating mines,” CEO Alberto Calderon said, “that are expected to provide high-margin ounces and unlock further value from our portfolio.”
The expansions would draw on existing plants and mine infrastructure to add output while limiting construction risk. They come as higher gold prices strengthen earnings, but rising costs and heavier investment absorb more of the cash generated by operations.
Geita
Geita accounts for most of the proposed spending, with $480 million to $580 million earmarked for work aimed at lifting annual output to about 600,000 oz. by 2030.
Plans include additional processing capacity and a paste backfill plant to open access to higher-grade underground ore, according to the results presentation .
At Cuiabá, spending of $200 million to $250 million would support roughly 75,000 additional ounces annually. Siguiri’s $70-million development program targets about 100,000 additional ounces a year through new pits supplying higher-grade ore.
Higher costs
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization rose 12% from a year earlier to $1.57 billion in the third quarter. AngloGold received an average $4,239 per oz. for its gold, up 21% from $3,490.
Free cash flow, however, fell 22% to $722 million as investment and tax payments increased and gold sales declined. The company ended September with net cash of $1.26 billion.
Total cash costs increased 3.6% from the second quarter to $1,534 an ounce. All-in sustaining costs reached $2,170 an ounce, 26% above a year earlier. Higher royalties and fuel costs contributed to cost pressures, alongside sustaining investment and lower production.
AngloGold maintained its annual production forecast of 2.8 million to 3.17 million oz. after producing 2.16 million oz. in the first nine months.
The company also disclosed that a worker died in an August rockfall at the Sukari underground mine in Egypt. Operations stopped for an investigation and have since resumed.
Shares closed Thursday 0.7% stronger at $88.56 in New York.

Three major packaging suppliers disclosed this week that they received federal grand jury subpoenas in September. International Paper and Smurfit Westrock said the Justice Department investigation in Chicago concerns the pricing and sale of containerboard, the paper used to make corrugated shipping boxes, and related products.
What’s Related
Smurfit Westrock received its subpoena Sept. 22, and International Paper received its subpoena Sept. 24. Packaging Corporation of America said it received a subpoena from the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division in late September seeking company records. All three companies say they are cooperating. Bloomberg reported that the Justice Department has not formally accused any of the companies or their employees of a crime.
“We are fully cooperating with the investigation,” Smurfit Westrock said in its quarterly filing. The company said it believes its business practices and those of its subsidiaries comply with U.S. antitrust laws.
Containerboard prices up by about 20%
Containerboard prices are about 20% higher than last year so far this year, according to Packaging Dive. The publication reported that International Paper and Smurfit Westrock were among the producers that announced three rounds of price increases this year.
The price buyers pay for finished boxes depends on their supplier agreements. Bloomberg reported that some contracts use a North American containerboard price index to help set prices.
A different lawsuit alleges price coordination
Suppliers can raise prices independently. A separate civil lawsuit filed in July 2025 alleges that major containerboard producers agreed to raise or maintain prices for containerboard and finished packaging products starting in November 2020. The suit also alleges that producers agreed to limit containerboard production capacity to push prices higher. The defendants dispute the allegations.
A federal judge denied a request to dismiss the civil case in September, allowing it to proceed. The plaintiff voluntarily dropped Smurfit Westrock plc from the lawsuit on Oct. 17, 2025, and could seek to add it back. Two of its subsidiaries remain defendants.

They Say SEMA Is Wild, This 700-HP Chevy S10 Hellcat Street Truck Runs Mid-Sevens (There's a Catch)

Photo: YouTube/VICtorious
Chevrolet’s light-duty pickup peak in engine size arrived with the 1990 C1500 454 SS, a 7.4-liter V8 bruiser wheezing out 230 horsepower for 15.7-second quarter-mile passes, while modern 6.2-liter Silverado 1500 trucks deliver 420 horsepower and 14.1-second sprints. Sadly, General Motors repeatedly failed to drop a Hemi V8 into its pickups. Corporate copyright infringement laws stop executives, leaving everyday gearheads limited strictly by their wallets. Meet the Chevy S10 Hellcat.
Before somebody yelled “hold my beer” and grabbed a welding torch, the humble Chevrolet S10 spent two generations hauling bags of garden mulch between 1982 and 2004. The first generation ran from 1982 to 1993, followed by a sleeker second generation from 1994 to 2004. For buyers craving factory rebellion with a bowtie badge, Chevrolet offered the 1994 to 1998 S10 SS and the ground-hugging 1999 to 2003 S10 Xtreme.
Those sporty Chevrolets packed a 4.3-liter Vortec V6 paired with either a 4L60-E 4-speed automatic or NV3500 5-speed manual transmission, mustering a polite 195 horsepower and 260 lb-ft of torque for a 7.8-second 0-to-60 mph jog and a 16.1-second quarter-mile at 86 mph. General Motors only went truly unhinged with the 1991 to 1992 GMC Syclone cousin, whose turbocharged 4.3-liter V6 made 280 horsepower for 13.4-second quarter-mile blasts.
Meanwhile, over at Chrysler’s asylum, engineers birthed the supercharged 6.2-liter Gen III Hemi V8, famous as the Hellcat, for the 2015 model year, retiring it from muscle cars in 2023 while keeping utility vehicles screaming through 2026. Force-fed by a 2.4-liter twin-screw supercharger, it initially unleashed 707 horsepower and 650 lb-ft of torque in the Dodge Challenger, Charger , and Jeep Grand Cherokee Trackhawk, before standard Dodge models hit 717 horsepower.
Photo: YouTube/VICtorious (@VICtoriousbuilds) Mopar stuffed that rowdy mill everywhere, rating it at 702 horsepower in the Ram 1500 TRX and 710 horsepower in the Dodge Durango, while 2.7-liter supercharged Redeye, Super Stock, and Jailbreak models delivered 797 to 807 horsepower. Following the 840-horsepower 2018 Demon, the 1,025-horsepower 2023 Challenger SRT Demon 170 clocked a neck-snapping 1.66-second 0 to 60 mph launch and an 8.91-second quarter-mile, while a 707-horsepower Mopar Hellcrate retails for $20,215.
In 2024, Victor Rafael, the mastermind behind the VICtorious and G2K Youtube channels, looked at his black first-generation S10 pickup, ironically nicknamed Sleepy Joe, and decided humanity had suffered enough predictable LS swaps. Craving 707 horsepower of supercharged Mopar blasphemy in a featherweight Chevy, Victor yanked the truck’s old LS V8 and 2-speed Powerglide, then hired Tom Kozlow, alias Street Racing Tom, to build a Turbo 400 3-speed automatic.
Forcing a Mopar engine to marry a General Motors gearbox required an SFI-certified J&W Performance adapter bellhousing. Next, the factory front-sump Hemi oil pan threatened to smash the S10 steering linkage, and since Victor refused to tube the front frame, he snagged a scarce Holley Gen III Hemi rear-sump pan from Summit Racing. With the doghouse removed, buddy Steve and fabricator Charles of Solo Man Motorsport wrestled the beast inside.
Photo: YouTube/VICtorious (@VICtoriousbuilds) Because massive Hemi cylinder heads left 0 inches of vertical wiggle room, lifting the engine 2 inches off standard clamshell mounts for removal was impossible. Instead, Charles modified Paul Horton’s Welder Series mounts with stationary rear tabs and bolt-in front plates, letting the V8 slide straight forward off the transmission dowels. Charles also inverted and plated the stock transmission crossmember bracket, while a shop shortened the driveshaft to 54.5 inches.
When the rear supercharger water manifold collided with the cab, Victor skipped buying a $429.95 Earl’s 1.875-inch manifold and introduced his firewall to an angle grinder, welding in custom sheet metal coated with primer, seam sealer, and satin black paint. Bulky SRT exhaust manifolds failed to fit, so he bought $329.95 Hooker Blackheart Hemi swap headers with V-band clamps and added Speedway Motors tubular upper arms with 1.5-inch ball joints.
Steering demanded creativity after the driver-side valve cover evicted the stock column pocket. Victor installed a modified TRZ Motorsports race column with a Delrin bushing, U-joints snaking past the header to the factory gearbox, a Strange quick-disconnect hub, and a Grant wheel. Up front, he trimmed 1 inch off the core support to fit an oversized radiator, dual electric fans, Gates hoses, and an oil cooler with a 90-degree adapter.
Photo: YouTube/VICtorious (@VICtoriousbuilds) Out in the bed beside two nitrous bottles, a Mitsubishi radiator, custom fan shroud, and intercooler pump push water through 0.75-inch lines to chill the blower. A rear fuel cell feeds stock rails via a MagnaFuel ProTuner 750 pump, Jegs 100-micron filter, E85-ready Evil Energy PTFE lines, Redhorse regulator, and Low Doller sensor. Electronics include a Holley Terminator X Max ECU, drive-by-wire Hemi pedal, vacuum block, and SmoothBoost bypass controller.
After Victor notched the frame for a 1-wire alternator, added a 3D-printed SR10 grille badge made by Mike from Backyard Shenanigans, and installed a 2006 to 2010 Charger mini-starter, the starter missed the flywheel. Shaving the starter face took 1 week and $120 at a machine shop. Worse, when the engine fired on a tune from Mike at Sinister Performance Club, it showed zero oil pressure from a trashed crankshaft.
Refusing to cry into his toolbox, Victor bought a refreshed 6.2-liter Hellcat engine making over 700 horsepower from Mike at Sinister Performance Club, while California wizard Richard Nedbal of FastManEFI assisted with calibration. On his birthday, Victor trailered Sleepy Joe on meaty Hoosier drag radials to Florida’s Immokalee Regional Raceway for a no-prep shootout, yanking both front wheels skyward, pedaling through ferocious tire smoke, and clocking a 7.50-second eighth-mile pass.

The affordable EV project is running behind schedule after new CEO Silvio Napoli said he wants it to be perfect before starting production. The release window is now expected for the second half of 2027. The EV startup desperately needs the affordable Cosmos to cut losses and help it survive.
While Rivian appears to be well on its way to profitability, its former peer Lucid Motors is still struggling to stay afloat. The major difference between the two EV startups is that Rivian is already selling the R2, a high-volume, affordable compact crossover. Lucid, on the other hand, is still working on its Cosmos rival, which should've launched later this year.
However, Lucid Motors is going through a painful reorganization, with a new management team that seeks to straighten the ailing ship. The new CEO, Silvio Napoli, who was appointed in June, announced in August that the Cosmos would not be rushed to market like the Air and Gravity were. Napoli set a new timeline for the second half of 2027.
Many are skeptical that Lucid Motors will be able to survive that long on its current cash reserves, which are depleting faster than expected. The third-quarter financial results will be announced on November 9. Still, previous quarters showed that Lucid is burning about $1.5 billion per quarter. The company had only $3,0 billion in cash at the end of June, which means it might run out by the time the Cosmos starts deliveries.
That didn't prevent Lucid from continuing work on the project. The startup teased the Cosmos at the end of a recent social media video, in a move aimed at showing that the project is still alive despite difficulties. This time, the teaser focuses on the crossover's light signature. At the rear, it shows red Lucid lettering integrated into the taillights and the rear light strip. Up front, the thin headlights appear to also be part of a light strip.
The silhouette matches the patent drawings that Lucid filed in May with the EU Intellectual Property Office. The drawings also had the Lucid lettering on the tailgate, as shown in the new teaser. We've seen the same light signature on prototypes Lucid has been testing in California recently. In fact, one of the prototypes also appears in the teaser video.

The Cosmos will be powered by a relatively small 69-kWh battery, but will be able to provide over 300 miles of range thanks to an impressive efficiency of up to 4.5 mi/kWh.
Lucid promised that the Cosmos would start under $50,000, although we know what that means for a new car model. The problem is that, by the end of 2027, Rivian will already sell a $45,000 R2 variant, while the Tesla Model Y starts well below that, at $39,900. Sarepta Therapeutics’ newly minted CEO Michael Severino laid out his path to returning the muscular dystrophy therapy maker to the forefront of the rapidly expanding market.
Sarepta Therapeutics’ new CEO Michael Severino has had 90 days to assess the path forward. With his Big Pharma lens, Severino thinks the biotech’s shift to effect size and quality clinical trials sites has set the muscular dystrophy therapy maker up to overcome the past few years of controversy.
During his first earnings call with the company on Thursday afternoon, Severino was asked for his opinion on Sarepta’s execution—given the biotech’s “mixed” history on clean clinical trial wins, as the analyst put it.
“One of the most important [things] is if you want to have a positive study, you need to have the most substantial effect size you can,” said Severino, who previously served in senior executive roles at AbbVie and Amgen.
Severino inherited a company that was emerging from a year of controversy. In 2025, multiple deaths were linked to Sarepta’s gene therapy programs, including the approved Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) treatment Elevidys. Sales of the therapy spiraled as the benefit-risk profile was questioned.

After a rocky 2025, Sarepta Therapeutics’ executives admit they have work to do to bring patients back into the fold as sales of Duchenne muscular dystrophy gene therapy Elevidys continue to decline.

In an attempt to move forward, Sarepta’s then CEO Doug Ingram signed a massive deal with Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals in November 2024, bringing in a new siRNA modality and mostly moving on from gene therapy.
Sarepta is also awaiting an FDA decision on the DMD exon skippers Vyondys 53 and Amondys 45. The company is seeking full approval of the treatments, which had each previously been granted accelerated approval by the FDA. But in November 2025, both failed confirmatory trials . Sarepta nevertheless resubmitted the package and a decision is expected in February 2027.
Enter Severino, with a tough job to do. He told analysts on Thursday that he’s satisfied with the work the company has been doing to improve clinical trials, including focusing on obtaining a bigger effect size to prove long-term benefit and better selection of clinical trial sites with the deep experience necessary to run a trial in a complex disease like DMD.
“I think we’ve gained significant experience as a company over the last many years in how to conduct studies in neuromuscular disease and how to pick those sites, and how to work with those sites to make sure we get quality data,” Severino said. “With respect to our study design and statistical capabilities, they are as good here as they are anywhere.”
The new CEO also expressed confidence in the upcoming siRNA programs from Arrowhead. Sarepta is preparing to initiate pivotal studies for SRP-1003 in myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) and SRP-1001 in facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD), both of which are expected to yield multiple ascending dose data by the end of this year.

source_document.body:
For decades, electric utilities have planned around a relatively predictable relationship between population growth, economic activity, weather and electricity consumption. Demand increased gradually, infrastructure investments followed long-term forecasts and utilities generally had time to prepare for changes in where and how electricity was consumed.
That planning model is being tested. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projected that commercial electricity sales would surpass residential sales in 2026, as overall U.S. electricity consumption reaches new highs. The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, growth in other large commercial facilities and continued electrification are reshaping the electricity landscape.
COMMENTARY
But the significance of this crossover extends well beyond which customer class consumes the most electricity. It signals a fundamental change in the scale, location and concentration of demand, one that challenges the assumptions utilities have relied on for decades.
A single large commercial customer can introduce hundreds of megawatts of new demand into a relatively small geographic area, sometimes on timelines that outpace the planning, permitting and construction of traditional grid infrastructure. At the same time, distributed energy resources (DERs), electric vehicles (EVs) and behind-the-meter technologies are making electricity flows increasingly dynamic.
The question is no longer simply how many additional megawatts the grid will need. Utilities must also understand where those megawatts are needed, when demand will materialize and how much capacity can be made available through better use of existing infrastructure.
Not All Grid Capacity Is Created Equal
One of the biggest challenges with commercial-led load growth is that available grid capacity is not evenly distributed. A utility may have sufficient generation resources or capacity across its broader service territory while facing significant constraints at the substations, feeders or transmission facilities serving a proposed commercial development. In other words, having enough electricity available in aggregate does not necessarily mean it can be delivered where a customer needs it.
Consider the scale of emerging AI infrastructure. Projects such as the Stargate-associated Crusoe data center campus in Abilene, Texas, illustrate the magnitude of the challenge, with development plans at approximately 1 gigawatt (GW). At that scale, accommodating new demand becomes a major transmission, generation and regional infrastructure planning consideration. While projects of this magnitude create significant transmission and regional planning challenges, the same fundamental questions about location, timing and available capacity also apply at the distribution level, where much smaller loads can create highly localized constraints.
But utilities do not need a gigawatt-scale project to encounter serious capacity constraints. Consider a commercial facility proposing to add 20 MW of demand within an existing distribution service area. Whether the utility can accommodate that load depends on the configuration and capacity of the surrounding network, including feeder and substation capabilities, transformer loading, voltage conditions, existing customer demand and the facility’s operating profile.
A feeder that appears to have available capacity during much of the year may approach its operating limits during a handful of summer afternoons. Another feeder may have more consistent headroom but require significant upgrades to support the customer’s full requested load. These distinctions matter because the infrastructure required to resolve each situation could be very different.
The first scenario might benefit from targeted load management or flexibility during constrained periods. The second may require physical upgrades regardless of how effectively existing resources are managed. Utilities must therefore move beyond simply estimating aggregate demand growth and toward understanding where and when new loads intersect with actual system constraints.
From Static Forecasting to Locational Grid Intelligence
Traditional load forecasting remains essential to utility planning. Long-term projections guide investments in generation, transmission, substations and other infrastructure that can take years to develop. However, the emerging load environment requires utilities to connect those long-range forecasts with a more granular understanding of distribution-system conditions.
Advanced metering infrastructure (AMI), grid-edge sensors, distribution automation systems and other operational technologies can provide utilities with a more detailed understanding of conditions across the distribution network. When combined with network models and analytics, these data sources can help utilities evaluate transformer and feeder loading, voltage conditions, localized demand peaks and the effects of distributed energy resources.
This information becomes particularly valuable when utilities connect it with advanced analytics and more dynamic forecasting models. Return to the example of a proposed 20 MW commercial load. A conventional planning approach might evaluate the customer’s requested peak demand against the capacity of the surrounding system. A more adaptive approach would examine how that demand is expected to develop and interact with existing grid conditions.
Will the facility require the full 20 MW immediately, or will its demand increase over several years? Will its peak coincide with the system’s existing summer peak? Are nearby customers adding EV charging, rooftop solar or battery storage? How will those resources affect the local load profile? Most importantly, is the resulting constraint persistent, or does it occur only during a limited number of high-stress hours?
These questions can produce very different investment decisions. For example, a feeder that exceeds its operating threshold for a few hours each year presents a different planning problem than one that is consistently overloaded. Both conditions require attention, but they do not necessarily require the same solution. More granular forecasting can help utilities distinguish between those situations, evaluate potential scenarios and identify where infrastructure investments will deliver the greatest benefit.
This is where grid-edge intelligence becomes especially important. Rather than relying exclusively on historical averages or system-level assumptions, utilities can use more detailed operational information to understand how their infrastructure is performing under actual conditions. That visibility does not create physical capacity on its own. It does, however, provide a stronger foundation for determining where additional investment is genuinely necessary.
Flexibility Becomes Part of the Capacity Equation
Once utilities understand where and when capacity constraints are likely to occur, another opportunity emerges: determining whether some portion of those constraints can be addressed using flexible resources already connected to the grid.
For years, demand response programs largely focused on reducing systemwide peak demand. Today, the growing number of distributed resources creates opportunities to apply flexibility more precisely, matching available resources with specific local grid needs. Residential batteries, smart thermostats, EV chargers, electric water heaters, distributed generation and controllable commercial loads can potentially reduce, shift or otherwise manage demand during constrained periods.
Consider a distribution feeder that experiences capacity limitations during several late-afternoon hours in August. If a utility can reliably coordinate nearby batteries, EV charging and other controllable loads during those periods, it may be able to reduce stress on the feeder without immediately rebuilding every affected asset.
That does not mean flexibility can replace traditional infrastructure. It cannot resolve every thermal limitation, voltage problem or reliability requirement, and a persistent capacity shortage will often demand physical upgrades.
But when the constraint is temporary, flexibility can become a valuable operational tool. The challenge is making that flexibility dependable enough to factor into planning and operational decisions. Five megawatts of enrolled flexible capacity sounds promising. But that number has limited value if the resources are not located behind the relevant constraint, cannot respond during the required hours or cannot sustain their response long enough to address the problem.
Utilities need to know not just how much flexibility exists, but how quickly it can respond and whether it performs as expected. This is where distributed energy resource management systems (DERMS) are becoming increasingly important. By coordinating distributed resources across customer programs and grid operations, DERMS can help utilities identify available flexibility, dispatch resources against specific system needs and measure their performance.
The distinction is important. A resource that participates in a broad demand response program may help reduce overall system peaks. A resource that can be reliably dispatched at a particular location and time can potentially help address a specific distribution constraint.
Moving from the first model to the second requires closer coordination between utility planning departments, grid operators and customer-facing energy programs. It also requires utilities to rethink how they value distributed resources. Rather than treating them exclusively as customer-owned technologies or program participation numbers, utilities can begin evaluating their contribution to system capacity, reliability and operational flexibility.
Build Where Necessary. Optimize Wherever Possible
One of the biggest challenges in planning for commercial load growth is uncertainty. Large commercial projects may be announced years before they reach full operation, and development timelines, energy requirements and even project viability can change along the way.
That creates a difficult balancing act for utilities. Investing too early in infrastructure for demand that is delayed or never materializes can place unnecessary costs on the system. Waiting too long, however, can create capacity constraints that slow economic development and limit the ability to serve new customers.
A more adaptive approach allows utilities to align infrastructure investments with how demand actually develops. This may include phased upgrades, closer coordination with large commercial customers and the strategic use of flexible resources to manage constraints while longer-term infrastructure is planned and built. The objective is not to avoid new construction, but to make more informed decisions about where, when and how much capacity to add.
Every Megawatt Has to Work Harder
The shift toward commercial-led electricity demand growth is changing more than how much capacity utilities need. It is changing how they must evaluate and plan for that capacity.
As large loads emerge in concentrated locations and on uncertain timelines, the ability to distinguish between immediate constraints, future requirements and opportunities to use existing infrastructure more effectively will become increasingly important.
For utilities, the challenge is no longer simply preparing for more megawatts. It is making sure every investment, and every available megawatt, delivers the greatest possible value as demand evolves.
— Nick Tumilowicz is director of Product Management, Distributed Energy Management Solutions, at Itron .

By: Northern Miner Staff November 6, 2026
Sherritt International (TSX: S) will temporarily lay off almost half its Canadian workforce to conserve cash while it seeks further United States approvals and financing to restart the Cuban operations that supply its Alberta refinery.
About 280 employees, representing 47% of Sherritt’s Canadian workforce, face layoffs expected to last about 90 days, although some could return sooner, the company said Wednesday . Metals refining at Fort Saskatchewan stopped June 22 after its feed inventory was depleted.
“This was a difficult decision, and we recognize the impact it will have on our employees and their families,” interim CEO Peter Hancock said.
Fuel deliveries
The layoffs underline how the refinery’s recovery depends on approvals and financing beyond Canada. A U.S. licence issued last month permits fuel deliveries to Moa in Cuba, but further authorization is needed to restart mining and processing and restore the flow of material to Alberta. Sherritt suspended direct participation in its Cuban joint ventures on May 7 following expanded U.S. sanctions. Fort Saskatchewan is one of only three nickel refineries in North America, the company says.
The initial licence, received from the United States Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control on Oct. 19, covers purchases and deliveries of fuel, fuel oil and sulphur, along with services provided by banks, vessel operators and insurers, Sherritt said in an Oct. 20 update. At that time, the first fuel shipment was expected to ship during the fourth quarter.
Multiple approvals
Sherritt has coordinated its applications with Gillon Capital, which is pursuing a potential controlling investment under a non-binding agreement. The fuel authorization is one of several approvals needed for that proposed transaction, the company said. Financing remains another obstacle. Sherritt warned in October of a material uncertainty that could cast significant doubt on its ability to continue as a going concern, with payments to suppliers and other obligations dependent on additional financing and a broader recapitalization.
Ammonia fertilizer and sulphuric acid production and sales will continue during the layoffs, along with maintenance, environmental protection and safety work, Sherritt said. Sherritt shares dropped 2.7% to 18¢ Thursday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about $127 million (US$91 million). They’ve lost about 24% of their value since the start of the year.

China has blocked SoftBank from buying ABB’s robotics business in the country, putting the $5.4 billion deal for ABB’s global robotics division in doubt. ABB, a Swiss industrial equipment maker, confirmed the decision on Nov. 5. It’s unclear whether the companies can carve out the Chinese business or otherwise restructure the deal.
What’s Related
“ABB and SoftBank are in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction,” ABB said. The Swiss company said SoftBank, which is responsible for securing regulatory approvals, had informed it of the decision by China’s foreign investment security review office. The office sits within China’s National Development and Reform Commission.
Why China said no
The Financial Times, which first reported the decision , said China’s competition review passed in February before the deal underwent a separate foreign investment security review. The newspaper reported that officials examined ABB’s Chinese supply chains and wanted some of the division’s robot manufacturing to stay in China.
Reuters reported that Chinese authorities were concerned about sensitive data being transferred to the United States. SoftBank declined to comment to Reuters, and the commission did not immediately respond to its request for comment.
What’s next
SoftBank signed the agreement in October 2025 and originally expected it to close in mid-to-late 2026, subject to regulatory approvals. The deal covers a business that designs, makes, and sells industrial robots and had about 7,000 employees when SoftBank announced the purchase.
China is ABB’s largest robotics market and accounts for about 30% of the division’s business. ABB opened a $150 million robotics factory and research center in Shanghai in 2022. The Financial Times reported that ABB makes more than 90% of the robots it sells to Chinese customers in China.
ABB and SoftBank are still working on the sale. Before signing with SoftBank, ABB had planned to list its robotics division as a standalone company in the second quarter of 2026. ABB dropped that plan when it agreed to the sale and gave no indication in its Nov. 5 update that it would revive it.

Agility Robotics , the maker of the Digit humanoid robot , began trading on Nasdaq on Thursday after closing its merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI. The company said the deal and related financing raised about $465 million before transaction expenses. Its shares trade under AGLT, and its warrants trade under AGLTW.
What’s Related
The Salem, Oregon, company plans to use the money to fill customer orders , build more robots, and put Digit to work at more sites. The total includes about $164 million from Churchill’s trust account, $201 million from a private investment led by Foxconn, and $100 million in equity funding Agility received before the merger closed on Nov. 4.
Agility says it’s the first U.S. publicly listed company focused solely on humanoid robots to have its machines in commercial use. “Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Agility Robotics CEO Peggy Johnson.
RELATED: Agility Robotics Unveils Digit 5 With Heavier Lift, Faster Charge
GXO expands usage of Digit
Agility’s robots have logged more than 65,000 hours of work at customer sites over nearly three years. Current customers include GXO, Schaeffler and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada. At GXO’s Flowery Branch, Georgia, facility, Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes since the companies signed a commercial agreement in 2024.
GXO plans to add Digit at sites in Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee, in early 2027. The agreement includes Agility Arc, cloud software that manages the robots and integrates them into customer operations. Agricultural equipment maker AGCO also signed an agreement for a pilot expected to start in 2027.
Three more manufacturers are paying to test Digit on specific jobs: a major global automaker, a large automotive parts developer, and a consumer products maker. The company says it’s also talking with more than 30 prospective customers.
Digit 5 will be widely available by 2028
Agility says it has more than $300 million in committed multiyear orders for Digit 5, the model it unveiled in September. The value of those orders depends on Agility meeting contract milestones and delivering the agreed features and specifications. The company expects early customers to get Digit 5 in the first half of 2027 and aims to make it widely available by year-end.
Agility designed Digit 5 to repeatedly lift up to 50 pounds and work closer to people. It can use different tools at the ends of its arms depending on the job. Agility says a Nyobolt battery recharges in nine minutes, which could give Digit 5 more than 20 hours of working time per day. The company plans to use NVIDIA’s IGX Thor computer in Digit 5 and expand its use of NVIDIA’s Halos safety technology .
Agility plans to build more robots at RoboFab, its 70,000-square-foot factory in Salem. The company says it designed the plant to produce up to 10,000 robots a year. It’s also adding a 50,000-square-foot site in Pittsburgh for software, AI , and customer support.
